content: Diseases of poverty are illnesses that disproportionately affect individuals living in poverty compared to those who are wealthier. In many instances, poverty itself serves as the primary risk factor for these diseases. Conversely, certain diseases can also contribute to or exacerbate poverty. The three most prominent diseases associated with poverty are AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis. Developing countries bear the overwhelming burden of these diseases, with 95% of global AIDS cases and 98% of active tuberculosis infections occurring in these regions. Additionally, 90% of malaria-related deaths are concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa. Collectively, these three diseases account for 10% of global mortality. Other diseases closely linked to poverty include measles, pneumonia, and diarrheal diseases, which are often grouped with AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis in broader discussions of poverty-related illnesses. Furthermore, infant and maternal mortality rates are significantly higher among impoverished populations. For instance, 98% of the 11,600 daily maternal and neonatal deaths occur in developing countries. Overall, diseases of poverty are responsible for approximately 14 million deaths annually. The mechanisms underlying the prevalence of these diseases among the poor are multifaceted. Factors such as overcrowded living conditions, inadequate sanitation, and higher rates of engagement in high-risk occupations, such as sex work, increase exposure to infectious diseases. Malnutrition, along with insufficient, inaccessible, or nonexistent healthcare, further impedes recovery and worsens disease outcomes. Malnutrition is implicated in 54% of childhood deaths from poverty-related diseases. Additionally, the lack of skilled healthcare providers during childbirth is a major contributor to the elevated maternal and infant mortality rates observed in impoverished communities. The consequences of diseases of poverty are profound and cyclical. These illnesses not only arise as a direct result of poverty but also perpetuate and deepen impoverishment by depleting personal and national health and financial resources. For example, malnutrition-related deaths among children are a daily tragedy that underscores the devastating impact of poverty on health. Certain diseases are also believed to actively cause poverty. Many of these are mental illnesses that impair social functioning, awareness, and cognitive abilities. Examples include autism, schizophrenia, antisocial personality disorder, and mental impairments resulting from substance abuse or trauma. Malaria is another disease that can contribute to poverty by reducing productivity and economic stability in affected regions.
